extracted.intended_audience: general literate readers; readers and writers of 19th‑century travel letters/essays (Tribune readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and informal guidance embedded in a 19th‑century travel‑letter/essay about how to write and read travel letters: emphasis on firsthand observation, moral purpose, balancing fact and fiction, and addressing readers' practical and ethical interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix fact with fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice that a reader (and by extension a writer) may combine factual material with fictional or embellished elements: 'Take fact with fiction, silver with the lead, And, at the mint, you can get gold instead; In fine, read me, even as you would be read.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a judicious blend of fact and imaginative shaping: the poem counsels readers to accept a mixture and writers to present material in a way that may transmute base elements into something valuable; implies stylistic license while asking for reciprocal reading generosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer firsthand experience to preserved substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Valorization of direct experience over secondhand, preserved versions: 'The best pleasure such a fruit can yield Is to be gathered in the open field; ... But the best pleasure such a fruit can yield Is to be gathered in the open field; If only as an article of food, Cherry or crab-apple is quite as good; And, for occasions of festivity, West India sweetmeats you had better buy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor original, on‑site observation and experiential detail in travel writing rather than relying on reports, summaries, or convenient substitutes (e.g., jam vs. fresh berries). The pleasure and value lie in authentic encounter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey what words cannot — use 'the language of eye and motion'
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim that close visual and behavioral observation communicates truths that verbal summary cannot: 'There is a language of eye and motion which cannot be put into words, and which teaches what words never can. I feel acquainted with the soul of this race; I read its nobler thought in their defaced figures.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show, don't merely tell: record gestures, looks, small actions, and nonverbal detail to reveal character and cultural soul; trust observational description to carry meaning beyond explicit exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance a central moral/intellectual purpose with attention to detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted counsel from The Dial distinguishing spiritual purpose from material detail: 'Is not the difference between spiritual and material things just this,--that in the one case we must watch details, in the other, keep alive the high resolve, and the details will take care of themselves? Keep the sacred central fire burning, and throughout the system, in each of its acts, will be warmth and glow enough.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a guiding principle or 'sacred central fire' (moral/intellectual aim) for the work while also attending to particulars; both high resolve and practical details are necessary for persuasive, wholesome writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address readers with substance and practical value
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that audiences (here, working classes using Mechanics' Institutes) prefer books of solid and permanent interest rather than mere amusement: 'the books in most constant demand are not those of amusement, but of a solid and permanent interest and value.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose with an eye to usefulness and lasting interest for the intended readership: provide material that educates, uplifts, or has durable worth rather than ephemeral entertainment alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write with educative and moral purpose for broader social improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit statement of the institutional educational aim: 'It is that I may help, be it ever so feebly, to train up a race of young men, who shall escape vice by rising above it; who shall love truth because it is truth, not because it brings them wealth or honor; who shall regard life as a solemn thing... who shall judge in all things for themselves, bowing the knee to no sectarian or party watchwords... and who, while they think for themselves, shall feel for others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame writing (and institutional program material) to cultivate character, independent judgment, social feeling, and civic responsibility — treat content as part of moral and civic education, not merely instruction in skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include vivid local anecdotes, customs, and material culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of concrete, local detail and small anecdotes (customs about bathing, museum contributions, statues, the launching of a boat, a phrenologist on board, etc.) to bring place and people to life: e.g., '_Mem._: None but the sick ever bathe in England' and descriptions of museum contributions from townspeople.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Populate travel writing with tangible, often small-scale particulars — customs, objects, local characters, museum pieces — to provide texture and credibility; these details serve both interest and ethnographic/human portrayal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to revise judgments after on‑site investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Author reports changing her opinion about a historical judgment after reading testimony and seeing the place: 'Now, upon the spot, having read all the testimony, I felt convinced that it should rest solely with the government... I change, and believe the country at large must, erelong, change from this opinion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow direct observation and primary-source investigation to alter earlier conclusions; travel writing should record not only impressions but the process by which views are tested and refined.
